Five Apple Watch models can measure your blood pressure and alert you to possible hypertension. However, the device will not provide actual blood pressure readings.

Some smart rings and other fitness devices can measure blood pressure, but they require periodic calibration with a traditional cuff-based blood pressure monitor. The upcoming Signal Ring claims to provide full blood pressure measurements without any calibration, and says clinical trials involving thousands of people support this claim...

"Silent killer"

Abnormally high (hypertension) as well as abnormally low (hypotension) blood pressure can pose significant health risks.

Of the two, hypertension is the most dangerous, which is why it is called a "silent killer" — because it can cause serious, irreversible damage to the arteries, heart and brain without any obvious symptoms. Many patients only learn they have the condition after suffering a heart attack or stroke.

Particularly for older people, it is advisable to monitor blood pressure regularly, and home cuff-based blood pressure monitors are also available on the market for convenient measurement. However, if it can be done fully automatically through a fitness device you are already wearing, that is undoubtedly the most ideal approach.

Apple Watch's blood pressure feature

The launch of watchOS 26 enables five Apple Watch models to measure blood pressure:

  • Apple Watch Series 11
  • Apple Watch Series 10
  • Apple Watch Series 9
  • Apple Watch Ultra 3
  • Apple Watch Ultra 2

However, these models will not provide any readings, and will only alert you when signs of possible high blood pressure are detected. Other devices such as the Oura Ring work in a similar way.

There are indeed fitness devices on the market that can provide actual blood pressure readings, but such devices need to be calibrated periodically with readings taken from a cuff-based blood pressure monitor.

Signal Ring

Startup Vital Signals has announced it has developed a smart ring called Signal Ring that can measure blood pressure as accurately as a traditional upper-arm cuff-based blood pressure monitor without any calibration.

According to Bloomberg, the company's CEO Tom Moss said he himself nearly died from undiagnosed hypertension, which led him to found the company.

The ring will be available for pre-order later today, shipping in October, priced at US$399, with no subscription required. Real-time blood pressure readings and long-term blood pressure trends will be displayed through the companion app (as shown above).

It is worth mentioning that the Oura Ring has not yet obtained approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), but clinical trials have shown that it can provide accurate blood pressure readings across thousands of participants.

Interestingly, Moss does not plan to market this ring to all consumers. He said its professional features are best suited for older people and groups assessed by doctors as being at risk of high blood pressure, implying that the Signal Ring is relatively less capable in other areas (such as sleep tracking).
